```{r challenge-setup, include=FALSE}
# One answer box per challenge. The walkthrough stays hidden until the
# correct answer is typed. The answer comes from the walkthrough's own code.
answer_box <- function(id, answer, example) {
  key <- jsonlite::base64_enc(tolower(gsub("\\s", "", answer)))
  sprintf(
'<div class="challenge-answer">
  <label for="input-%1$s"><strong>Your answer</strong> (e.g. <code>%3$s</code>):</label>
  <input id="input-%1$s" type="text" autocomplete="off" data-key="%2$s" data-target="%1$s">
  <button type="button" class="challenge-check" data-check="%1$s">Check</button>
  <span class="challenge-feedback" id="feedback-%1$s"></span>
</div>', id, key, example)
}

# All paths are relative to the folder of this page (the repo root), whatever
# the working directory is when knitting.
page_dir <- dirname(normalizePath(knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE)))

# Knit one walkthrough from challenges/walkthroughs.Rmd and return its content
# and its answer. Each walkthrough starts at a line "<!-- walkthrough: id -->".
knit_walkthrough <- function(id, file = "challenges/walkthroughs.Rmd") {
  path <- file.path(page_dir, file)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    stop("Can't find the walkthroughs: ", path,
         "\nIt must be in a folder 'challenges' next to home_challenges.Rmd.")
  }
  lines   <- readLines(path, encoding = "UTF-8")
  markers <- grep("^<!-- walkthrough: [A-Za-z0-9_-]+ -->$", lines)
  ids     <- sub("^<!-- walkthrough: ([A-Za-z0-9_-]+) -->$", "\\1", lines[markers])
  if (!id %in% ids) stop("No walkthrough with id '", id, "' in ", path)
  start <- markers[ids == id] + 1
  end   <- c(markers[-1] - 1, length(lines))[ids == id]
  env <- new.env()
  # run the walkthrough code from the repo root, so data paths work
  old_root <- knitr::opts_knit$get("root.dir")
  knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = page_dir)
  on.exit(knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = old_root))
  content <- knitr::knit_child(text = lines[start:end], envir = env, quiet = TRUE)
  if (!exists("answer", envir = env)) stop("Walkthrough '", id, "' does not define `answer`")
  list(content = content, answer = env$answer)
}

# Print the hidden walkthrough block
walkthrough_block <- function(id, wt) {
  cat("\n\n::: {#walkthrough-", id, " .walkthrough}\n\n",
      "#### 🔓 Solution walkthrough {-}\n\n",
      wt$content, "\n\n:::\n\n", sep = "")
}
```

One short data challenge per day, each with **one exact answer**. Type it in the box to check it: the correct answer unlocks a solution walkthrough.

<div class="alert alert-info">
  <strong>Work in pairs, use the hints, and try before you peek.</strong> The solutions are also in the course repository, but you'll learn much more by getting there yourself. Thursday's challenge is the hardest: you have until Friday at 12:00. We'll go through all answers in Friday's discussion.
</div>

<!-- ======================= MONDAY: Countable Colonies ======================= -->

```{r wt-colonies, include=FALSE}
wt_colonies <- knit_walkthrough("colonies")
```

::: {.challenge-card}

### 🧫 Monday · Countable Colonies {-}

<p class="challenge-meta">Beginner · ~30 min · Monday: data types, operators, vectors</p>

**The scenario.** You diluted a bacterial culture 1,000 to 1,000,000 times, spread 0.1 mL of each dilution on three plates, and counted the colonies the next day. Some plates were too crowded to count: you wrote `TNTC` (too numerous to count).

**Your task.** Estimate the concentration of the culture in colony-forming units per mL (CFU/mL):

- only use plates with **30 to 300 colonies** (the countable range),
- for each of those plates, CFU/mL = colonies ÷ (dilution × volume plated),
- take the **mean** of these values.

Report **log10 of the mean CFU/mL, rounded to 2 decimals** (e.g. `7.12`). `log10()` works like `log2()`, with base 10.

<details>
  <summary>Get the data</summary>
Copy these lines into R:
```{r, code=readLines(file.path(page_dir, "data/challenges/colonies.R")), eval=FALSE}
```
</details>

<details>
  <summary>Hint 1</summary>
What type is `colonies`? What happens when you convert it with `as.numeric()`?
</details>

<details>
  <summary>Hint 2</summary>
Build one logical vector that is `TRUE` for countable plates, and use it to select from **both** `colonies` and `dilution`.
</details>

```{r, results='asis', echo=FALSE}
cat(answer_box("colonies", wt_colonies$answer, "7.12"))
```

```{r, results='asis', echo=FALSE}
walkthrough_block("colonies", wt_colonies)
```

:::

<!-- ======================= TUESDAY: Mouse Mismatch ======================= -->

```{r wt-mice, include=FALSE}
wt_mice <- knit_walkthrough("mice")
```

::: {.challenge-card}

### 🐭 Tuesday · Mouse Mismatch {-}

<p class="challenge-meta">Beginner+ · ~45 min · Tuesday: data frames, loading data, basic statistics</p>

**The scenario.** You weighed 20 mice. The scale exported the weights from one computer; the animal facility sent the genotypes (wild type, `WT`, or knockout, `KO`) from another. Do knockout mice weigh more?

**Your task.** Combine the two files and compare the weight of KO and WT mice with a Welch t-test (the default in `t.test()`). Report the **p-value, rounded to 3 decimals**.

<details>
  <summary>Get the data</summary>
```{r, eval=FALSE}
download.file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NBISweden/workshop-r/master/data/challenges/mouse_weights.csv",
              "data/mouse_weights.csv")
download.file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NBISweden/workshop-r/master/data/challenges/mouse_genotypes.csv",
              "data/mouse_genotypes.csv")
```
</details>

<details>
  <summary>Hint 1</summary>
Look at both files with `readLines()` before you read them. Do they use the same separator and decimal mark?
</details>

<details>
  <summary>Hint 2</summary>
Are the mice in the same order in both files? Does every ID appear in both files? (`x %in% y` checks, for each element of `x`, whether it is in `y`.) After merging, how many rows do you have?
</details>

```{r, results='asis', echo=FALSE}
cat(answer_box("mice", wt_mice$answer, "0.123"))
```

```{r, results='asis', echo=FALSE}
walkthrough_block("mice", wt_mice)
```

:::

<!-- ======================= WEDNESDAY: Primer Pairs ======================= -->

```{r wt-primers, include=FALSE}
wt_primers <- knit_walkthrough("primers")
```

::: {.challenge-card}

### 🧬 Wednesday · Primer Pairs {-}

<p class="challenge-meta">Intermediate · ~45 min · Wednesday: loops and functions (tidyverse optional)</p>

**The scenario.** A colleague designed forward (`F`) and reverse (`R`) qPCR primers for 30 genes and typed them into a spreadsheet. Before ordering, you check which pairs are good.

**Your task.** A primer pair **passes** if:

- both primers have a **GC content of 40–60 %**,
- both primers have a **melting temperature (Tm) of 52–60 °C**, using the Wallace rule: Tm = 2 × (A + T) + 4 × (G + C),
- the two Tm values differ by **at most 2 °C**.

Report the **number of passing pairs** and the **target of the passing pair with the highest mean Tm**, joined by a dash (e.g. `7-GAPDH`).

<details>
  <summary>Get the data</summary>
```{r, eval=FALSE}
download.file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NBISweden/workshop-r/master/data/challenges/primers.csv", "data/primers.csv")
```
</details>

<details>
  <summary>Hint 1</summary>
Write a function that takes **one** sequence and counts its G/C and A/T bases. `substr(seq, i, i)` gives the base at position `i`, and a `for` loop over `1:nchar(seq)` visits every position. Test it on a sequence where you know the answer, e.g. `"GGCCAATT"`. Then use a second loop to run it on every primer.
</details>

<details>
  <summary>Hint 2</summary>
Look closely at the data before you start. `table(primers$direction)` and `head(primers$sequence)` are good places to look. Is everything written the same way?
</details>

<details>
  <summary>Hint 3</summary>
To compare the two primers of a pair, put them in the same row: make one data frame of forward primers and one of reverse primers, and `merge()` them by target.
</details>

```{r, results='asis', echo=FALSE}
cat(answer_box("primers", wt_primers$answer, "7-GAPDH"))
```

```{r, results='asis', echo=FALSE}
walkthrough_block("primers", wt_primers)
```

:::

<!-- ======================= THURSDAY: Who's the Imposter? ======================= -->

```{r wt-imposter, include=FALSE}
wt_imposter <- knit_walkthrough("imposter")
```

::: {.challenge-card}

### 🕵️ Thursday · Who's the Imposter? {-}

<p class="challenge-meta">Advanced · due Friday 12:00 · Thursday: base graphics, ggplot2, plus the whole week</p>

**The scenario.** You received RNA-seq counts for 12 mouse liver samples, with a sample sheet. Something went wrong in the lab: **one sample is mislabelled**. Its sex in the sample sheet doesn't match its biology.

**Your task.** Find the mislabelled sample.

- Normalise the counts to **counts per million (CPM)**: divide each sample's counts by its total counts (all genes in the file), times 1,000,000.
- Use sex-specific genes: *XIST* is expressed in female cells; *RPS4Y1*, *DDX3Y*, *KDM5D*, *UTY* and *EIF1AY* are on the Y chromosome, so they are expressed in male cells only.
- Make a plot that shows the problem.

Report the **sample ID** and its **RPS4Y1 expression in CPM, rounded to a whole number**, joined by a dash (e.g. `S01-123`).

**Bonus (no answer box):** two samples have a second problem. Can you find it?

<details>
  <summary>Get the data</summary>
```{r, eval=FALSE}
download.file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NBISweden/workshop-r/master/data/challenges/counts.csv", "data/counts.csv")
download.file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NBISweden/workshop-r/master/data/challenges/sample_sheet.csv", "data/sample_sheet.csv")
```
</details>

<details>
  <summary>Hint 1</summary>
Read `counts.csv` with `row.names = 1`, so the gene names become row names. `colSums()` gives the library size of each sample. Are they similar? To divide each column by its own total, loop over the samples, or transpose with `t()`, divide, and transpose back.
</details>

<details>
  <summary>Hint 2</summary>
For each sample, you need the CPM of *XIST* and the CPM of the Y genes (e.g. their mean), plus the sex from the sample sheet. Put them in one data frame, then plot *XIST* against the Y genes, coloured by sex.
</details>

<details>
  <summary>Hint 3 (bonus)</summary>
`cor()` on the CPM matrix compares every sample with every other sample. Can you show the result as a plot?
</details>

```{r, results='asis', echo=FALSE}
cat(answer_box("imposter", wt_imposter$answer, "S01-123"))
```

```{r, results='asis', echo=FALSE}
walkthrough_block("imposter", wt_imposter)
```

:::

<!-- To add a challenge: see the instructions at the top of challenges/walkthroughs.Rmd -->

<script>
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () {
  function normalise(s) { return s.trim().toLowerCase().replace(/\s+/g, ""); }
  function check(id) {
    var input = document.getElementById("input-" + id);
    var feedback = document.getElementById("feedback-" + id);
    var walkthrough = document.getElementById("walkthrough-" + id);
    var guess;
    try { guess = btoa(normalise(input.value)); } catch (e) { guess = ""; }
    if (guess === input.dataset.key) {
      feedback.textContent = "✅ Correct! The walkthrough is unlocked below.";
      walkthrough.classList.add("unlocked");
    } else {
      feedback.textContent = "❌ Not quite. Check the hints, and try again!";
    }
  }
  document.querySelectorAll("[data-check]").forEach(function (button) {
    button.addEventListener("click", function () { check(button.dataset.check); });
  });
  document.querySelectorAll(".challenge-answer input").forEach(function (input) {
    input.addEventListener("keydown", function (e) {
      if (e.key === "Enter") check(input.dataset.target);
    });
  });
});
</script>
